list.listitem: Graves' disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism. C

Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) has a sensitivity of greater than 98% and specificity of greater than 92% when used to confirm suspected thyroid disease and is the best initial laboratory test for thyroid dysfunction. C
Radioactive iodine (RAI) is increasingly used as first-line therapy in the United States, with surgery reserved for special populations. B
Antithyroid drugs (ATDs) alone rarely achieve permanent remission of hyperthyroidism, but are useful in managing hyperthyroidism prior to definitive therapy with RAI or surgery. B
Potential serious morbidities of hyperthyroidism include ophthalmopathy, atrial fibrillation, congestive heart failure (CHF), stroke, seizure, and osteopenia/osteoporosis. C

background.definition: Hyperthyroidism is a condition in which there is excessive thyroid hormone action.

list.listitem: 0.5 per 1000 persons per year.
2% of women.
0.2% of men.
Five to 10 times more common in women than in men.
Subclinical thyroid disease is more common than overt disease in the primary care population, occurring in 1% of men older than 60 years and 1.5% of women older than 60.5 years.
Hyperthyroidism due to Graves' disease is one of the most common autoimmune disorders, affecting more than 3 million people in the United States.

In a US community population study, there was a trend toward increased hip fracture incidence in men with subclinical hyperthyroidism (13.65/1000 men-years vs 5/1000 men-years for euthyroid men); adjusted OR = 3.27 (0.99-11.30). There was no clear association between subclinical thyroid dysfunction and hip fracture in women.
Graves' disease: autoimmune thyroid disease characterized by toxic diffuse goiter; 80% of hyperthyroidism cases.
Toxic adenoma (Plummer's disease).
Toxic multinodular goiter (MNG).
Painful subacute thyroiditis.
Silent thyroiditis (eg, postpartum).
Iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (eg, amiodarone; Jod-Basedow phenomenon).
Excessive pituitary TSH.
Trophoblastic disease or germ cell tumor with excessive human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG).
Excessive ingestion of thyroid hormone (factitious thyrotoxicosis).
Struma ovarii: presence of functional thyroid tissue in an ovarian tumor.
Medication induced (eg, Interferon and check-point inhibitors)

Graves' disease is due to pathologic stimulation of the thyroid gland by antibodies to the TSH receptor. The ophthalmopathy of Graves' disease is caused by deposition of glycosaminoglycans in the retroorbital tissues with T-cell activation. Orbital fibroblasts are thought to be targets of autoimmune attack in the disease.
Plummer's disease is due to an autonomously functioning thyroid nodule.
Thyroiditis causes hyperthyroidism due to inflammation/destruction of thyroid cells with release of preformed thyroid hormones.

Iodine load can cause hyperthyroidism in patients with underlying toxic nodular goiter due to increased thyroid hormone synthesis by an autonomously functioning thyroid nodule; this is more common in areas of iodine deficiency.
Excessive pituitary TSH stimulates excessive thyroid hormone production.
Trophoblastic disease may cause hyperthyroidism due to excessive HCG stimulating the TSH receptor.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Family history (15% of patients with Graves' disease have an affected relative)
Age (Graves' disease: peak age 20-40 years; toxic MNG: peak age 55 years)
Relocation from iodine-deficient to iodine-sufficient area
Polymorphisms of interleukin-1 alpha (Asian population) OR = 2.07 (Graves' disease) and 3.22 (Graves' ophthalmopathy)
Polymorphisms of Foxp3 gene (Asian population), OR = 1.3 (Graves’ disease)
Polymorphism of promotor region of TNF-α gene (European population), OR =1.97 (Graves’ disease)

list.listitem: The USPSTF found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against routine screening for thyroid disease in the primary care setting.B In one study, universal screening of pregnant women did not result in a decrease in adverse outcomes.

While some groups are at increased risk (eg, postpartum women, people with Down's syndrome, the elderly), it is not clear that screening in these higher risk groups leads to improved outcomes compared with waiting for symptoms to appear. B
Patients with long-standing hyperthyroidism or subclinical hyperthyroidism have increased rates of osteoporosis and osteopenia; bone mineral density should be assessed and appropriately managed. C

Smoking cessation is recommended, as smoking is associated with increased risk of developing Graves' ophthalmopathy and increased relapse rate in patients with Graves' disease after completing a course of antithyroid medications. C
History and physical examination are typical for signs and symptoms of excessive thyroid hormone action (see ). C
Thyroid function tests show suppressed TSH with elevated T4 and/or T3 levels. C

Radioiodine uptake is increased in Graves' disease and in toxic nodular goiter and low or absent uptake is seen in subacute thyroiditis or exogenous thyroid hormone ingestion. These tests are helpful if the diagnosis is uncertain. C
Thyroid peroxidase antibodies and TSH receptor antibodies are helpful in differentiating autoimmune Graves' disease from toxic MNG. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Cachexia, fevers, malaise, other systemic or local findings
Hyperglycemia, obesity if type 2 diabetes mellitus, polydipsia, polyuria, neuropathy, retinopathy
Age, episodes of hot flashes, history of waning menses
Orthostatic hypotension, hyponatremia, nausea/abdominal pains, risk factors

list.listitem: Common signs and symptoms (>50% prevalence) include tachycardia, fatigue, weight loss, increased appetite, goiter, tremor, nervousness, hyperreflexia, increased sweating, heat intolerance, and polydipsia.
Elderly patients may present with apathetic symptoms including anorexia and fatigue, and all elderly patients with atrial fibrillation should be screened for hyperthyroidism.

Ophthalmopathy may be present in Graves' disease; features include proptosis (anterior displacement of the eye with protrusion), extraocular muscle dysfunction (diplopia, visual field deficits), lid retraction/lid lag (with increased area of visible sclera and corneal exposure keratitis or ulcer due to incomplete eyelid closure), periorbital edema, chemosis (conjunctival swelling), and scleral injection.
Goiter is present in up to 90% of patients (age <70 years) with hyperthyroidism; goiter is present in 50% of older patients (age >70 years).

In a retrospective chart review of 12,366 ED patients who underwent laboratory testing for thyroid disease, 0.8% were diagnosed with hyperthyroidism or thyrotoxicosis. The sensitivity and specificity of tachycardia for hyperthyroidism were 70% and 62%, LR+ 1.8 and LR- 0.5.
TSH less than 0.1 mU/L has greater than 98% sensitivity and greater than 92% specificity in confirming suspected thyroid disease.

A large cross-sectional study found that normal ranges change with age. For example, 20- to 30-year-olds will have a TSH level of between 0.44 and 4.49 mIU/L, while people 70 years to 85 years of age will have a TSH between 0.41 and 6.48 mIU/L.
Elevated T4 (or free T4 [FT4]) with low TSH confirms hyperthyroidism; rarely (3%-5% of patients), a patient may have normal or low T4 but elevated T3 and low TSH (T3 thyrotoxicosis).
A normal T4 and T3 but low TSH indicates subclinical hyperthyroidism.
TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) have a positive and negative likelihood ratio of 247 and 0.01, respectively, for diagnosing Graves' disease and are the preferred diagnostic test for that condition.

Thyroid peroxidase antibodies (present in 70%-80% of patients with Graves' disease) and TSH receptor antibodies (TBII = thyroid binding inhibitory immunoglobulin) may also be useful in differentiating between Graves' disease and toxic MNG.

Biotin supplement intake interferes with the accuracy of thyroid function tests, leading to falsely elevated FT4,TSH receptor antibodies, and low TSH. Therefore, in patients with biochemical profiles suggestive of hyperthyroidism without clinical correlation, biotin intake must be ruled out

Thyroid uptake and scan: radioiodine uptake to evaluate degree of thyroid gland (hyper)activity, and thyroid scan to assess the distribution of functional tissue within the thyroid gland. These tests are of value in excluding thyroiditis and preventing inappropriate treatment of thyroiditis with ATDs or ablative therapy with radioiodine or surgery. Nuclear imaging is also of value in directing therapy because it can differentiate Graves' disease, which may remit after ATDs, from toxic MNG, which is a permanent condition that does not remit with ATDs.
Thyroid ultrasound with color flow Doppler is useful to distinguish nodular forms of Graves' disease from nodular nonautoimmune causes of hyperthyroidism.
Examine the thyroid to assess consistency, size, and presence of nodules.
Order TSH, thyroxine (T4), and triiodothyronine (T3) tests to establish the diagnosis of hyperthyroidism. If TSH is low but T3 and free T4 are normal, repeat labs in 4 to 6 months.

If stigmata of Graves' Disease, diagnosis it. If no stigmata, obtain TSH-receptor antibody. If that is elevated, diagnose Graves' disease. If TSH-receptor antibody is normal, obtain thyroid scintgraphy.
Diffusely increased uptake: diagnose Graves' disease Focal areas of increased uptake: toxic adenoma or toxic multinodular goiter Low or absent uptake: If suspicion for exogenous thyroid exposure or intake, measure serum thyroglobulin. If no suspicion, diagnose thyroiditis.
Thyroid ultrasound can be used to evaluate nodules and goiter.
Radioiodine uptake and thyroid scan can be used, if necessary, to differentiate between etiologies of hyperthyroidism ().
ATDs are useful initial therapy for achieving euthyroidism, but due to high relapse rate, RAI ablation or surgery are regarded as more definitive therapies for permanent cure of hyperthyroidism. A

Radioactive iodine (RAI) is increasingly used as first-line therapy in the United States, with surgery reserved for special populations; risk of Graves' ophthalmopathy is increased following RAI versus ATD. B
Use beta blockers for symptomatic control of adrenergic symptoms. A
Glucocorticoids are indicated for management of severe ophthalmopathy, especially in patients undergoing RAI. Teprotumumab is a new and effective but expensive treatment option for ophthalmopathy. B
ATDs: propylthiouracil (PTU) and methimazole (MMI) inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis by blocking thyroid peroxidase; PTU also inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.

Evidence suggests that the optimal duration of ATD is 12 to 18 months.A low-dose titration regimen has similar efficacy to the high-dose regimen with fewer adverse effects; continued thyroxine treatment appears to offer no advantages.
Combining an ATD with potassium iodide until free T4 normalizes may speed resolution of hyperthyroidism.

A high relapse rate (>50%) is seen when ATD is stopped. In one RCT (N = 191), relapse was significantly decreased by adding a 3-month course of intrathyroid injections of 5 mg dexamethasone (twice weekly into both lobes in month 7, weekly in month 8, and twice a month in month 9 of an 18-month MMI course). The 2-year relapse rate was 7.4% in the injection plus MMI group versus 51% with MMI alone.
Compared to surgery and RAI, ATD use in the treatment of Grave's disease is associated with a much higher relapse rate (52.7% with ATD vs 15% with RAI and 10% with surgery).

ATDs may diminish the efficacy of RAI, and treatment failure rate is higher if an ATD is used continuously until the time of radioiodine administration. Studies indicate decreased failure rate when the ATD is withdrawn 2 to 14 days prior to RAI ablation.
Side effects of ATDs include skin rash (3%-5%), arthralgias, myalgias, and idiopathic granulocytopenia (0.5%); severe hepatitis occurs rarely (0.1%).
Use propranolol to control beta-adrenergic symptoms of hyperthyroidism.
Glucocorticoids are recommended to manage ophthalmopathy, especially if therapy with RAI is planned.

American Thyroid Association and the European Thyroid Association guidelines recommend the use of rituximab and tocilizumab in the management of steroid-resistant disease. In a RCT of 32 patients with moderate-to-severe steroid-resistant Graves ophthalmopathy, treatment with tocilizumab vs placebo showed a statistically significant improvement in clinical activity score (CAS) by ≥ 2 points (OR 9.8, p = 0.04) at week 16 post-treatment compared with baseline

American Thyroid Association and European Thyroid Association guidelines recommend 6-month course of 100 microgram oral selenium twice daily for management of mildly-active graves ophthalmopathy particularly in regions of selenium insufficiency. In a single-center RCT, treatment of mild Graves ophthalmopathy with 100 microgram of oral selenium for 6 months showed a statistically significant improvement in disease activity (CAS decreased from 2.9 to 1.4) compared with placebo

A monoclonal antibody called teprotumumab (Tepezza) has been approved by the FDA and is given as a series of 8 infusions over 21 weeks. In an RCT with 42 patients, it was highly effective with patients receiving the active drug much more likely to achieve a clinical activity score of 0 or 1 (59% vs 21%, NNT = 3). However, the cost is approximately $15,000 per infusion for a total cost of $120,000 for a course of 8 infusions. A systematic review of 3 studies with 341 total patients confirmed its efficacy but also noted adverse events including muscle spasms and gastrointestinal symptoms.
Topical cyclosporine (0.05%) was helpful in one case series for thyroid-related dry eye symptoms.
With increased data regarding efficacy and safety of RAI for hyperthyroidism, surgery is falling out of favor as first-line therapy in the United States.

Thyroidectomy remains useful as definitive therapy in pediatric patients with Graves' disease, pregnant women unable to tolerate ATDs or receive radioiodine therapy, patients with large goiters causing compressive symptoms, or patients with concomitant thyroid cancer.

A systematic review identified 6 studies with 846 patients comparing endoscopic with open thyroidectomy. Endoscopic thyroidectomy had less blood loss (32 ml, 95% CI 27-37) and better cosmetic outcomes, but higher costs and longer operative time.
A randomized trial in 205 patients comparing near total thyroidectomy with total thyroidectomy found no difference in any of the outcomes evaluated.
Giving a short course of potassium iodide pre-operatively was associated with lower blood loss (50 vs 140 ml) in a randomized trial.
Potential complications are hypoparathyroidism and vocal cord paralysis.
Rate of hypothyroidism with surgery is 28% to 43% after 10 years.
Hyperthyroidism recurs in 10% to 15% of patients after subtotal thyroidectomy.

Radioactive iodine (RAI) ablation of the thyroid is increasingly used as first-line therapy for hyperthyroidism. Euthyroidism is achieved in 80% of patients after a single dose of RAI. For example, an Australian series of 92 patients with 10 year follow-up found that 79% achieved remission with a single dose, and of those receiving a second dose, 12 of 19 were hypothyroid as a result.

However failure of RAI is more likely in patients with higher thyroid volume (>50 ml) and higher RAI 5 and 24 hour uptake (>0.8), with failure rates of 70% and 42% respectively. A study of 167 patients with Grave's disease treated with radioactive iodine found that 50% became eythyroid and 38% hypothyroid. Treatment failure was associated with having a 2 hour radiactive iodine uptake >58.5% (OR 4.1, 95% CI 2.0-7.8).

An RCT including 64 patients with post-RAI relapsed hyperthyroidism showed that long-term methimizole (MMI) treatment is superior to RAI due to faster achievement of euthyroid state and sustained improvement of hyperthyroidism over the 60-month follow-up period
Hypothyroidism occurs in up to 50% of patients within the first year after RAI and subsequently at a rate of 2% per year.
Iodine from contrast dye may decrease efficacy of RAI; RAI should be deferred for at least 2 months after an iodinated contrast dye study.
Patients with severe ophthalmopathy should be treated with concomitant glucocorticoids to prevent possible worsening of ophthalmopathy following RAI.

The risk of developing new or worsening Graves' ophthalmopathy ranges from 20% to 46% after RAI and 5% to 28% after ATD. The risk of developing severe ophthalmopathy after RAI is about 7%; risk appears increased in smokers. In 1 small RCT of RAI versus ATD, there was difference in progression or development of ophthalmopathy at 1 year in patients with Graves' disease and mild or no eye disease at baseline.
Severe thyrotoxicosis with hemodynamic compromise (thyroid storm).
Severe ophthalmopathy with visual compromise.
Severe ophthalmopathy: glucocorticoids are first-line therapy, with surgical decompression of orbits or orbital radiation considered if glucocorticoids fail. Smoking cessation is recommended.
Untreated hyperthyroidism can lead to atrial fibrillation and CHF.
Patients with subclinical hyperthyroidism are at an increased risk of fracture (HT 1.4, 95% CI 1.1-1.6).
There is also an increased risk of seizures (0.2% in 1 study) and ischemic stroke (1% vs 0.6%).

Patients with MNG appear to have a higher cardiovascular risk than patients with Graves' disease, although patients with Graves' disease have autoimmune cardiac complications such as valve involvement, pulmonary arterial hypertension, and specific cardiomyopathy.

Patients with hyperthyroidism may be at increased risk of thyroid cancer; in 1 Turkish case series, thyroid malignancy rates were 16% in patients with MNG, 6.4% in those autonomous functioning nodules, and 12.6% in patients with Graves' disease.
Hyperthyroidism is associated with an increased risk of anemia (OR 1.7, 95% CI 1.00-2.87).

Thyroid storm: ICU management; therapy to inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis and release, including PTU, dexamethasone, iodine (SSKI or sodium iodide); beta blockers for symptom control; antipyretic with acetaminophen (avoid salicylates).
Continued monitoring of thyroid function tests after treatment for hyperthyroidism is warranted due to greater than 50% relapse after withdrawal from ATDs. B
There is a high frequency of hypothyroidism after RAI or thyroidectomy. A
Untreated Graves' disease may have a waxing/waning cycle over years.
Toxic MNG/adenoma are permanent conditions and do not remit spontaneously.
Untreated hyperthyroidism may progress to thyroid storm, a life-threatening complication.
Untreated hyperthyroidism can lead to atrial fibrillation, CHF, and osteoporosis.
Patients with subclinical hyperthyroidism are at increased risk for fracture (HR 1.4, 95% CI 1.1-1.6).

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis may occur in the setting of hyperthyroidism and is associated with hypokalemia. It occurs more commonly in men (male:female ratio 130:5). Only 17% of patients have symptomatic hyperthyroidism prior to the onset of paralysis and most patients have no clear precipitating event.

Smoking, presence of goiter, higher pretreatment levels of T4, larger thyroid volume, and greater disease activity as measured by TBI and TRAb levels predict a greater likelihood of recurrence in patients with Graves' disease.

In a follow-up study (mean 41 months) of 102 elderly women with subclinical hyperthyroidism and TSH between 0.1 and 0.4 mIU/L, progression to clinical hyperthyroidism was uncommon (approximately 1% per year) and spontaneous TSH normalization occurred in 24%. Most had persistent subclinical hyperthyroidism.
Levels of TSH receptor antibodies are predictive of remission after ATD therapy, and high antibody levels are associated with a severe course of Graves' ophthalmopathy.

Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) is strongly correlated with Graves' ophthalmopathy activity and severity; clinical sensitivity (97% vs 77%; P <0.001) and specificity ( 89% vs 43%; P <0.001) of a novel chimeric (Mc4)/TSI appears greater than TSH receptor antibodies.
Quality of life is decreased in patients with Graves' ophthalmopathy, regardless of type of hyperthyroid treatment.
Approximately one-third of patients become hypothyroid within 20 years of treatment with an ATD and 80% of patients become hypothyroid after a single dose of RAI.

During ATD treatment, perform thyroid function tests every 3 to 4 months; after the ATD treatment course, check thyroid function tests every 3 months for 1 year, then every 6 months for 1 year, and then annually.
After RAI, check thyroid function tests every 4 weeks and treat for hypothyroidism if/when TSH becomes elevated.
Patients treated successfully for hyperthyroidism require lifelong surveillance for onset of hypothyroidism or recurrence of hyperthyroidism.
Elderly patients may present with nonspecific fatigue and weight loss in the absence of other typical symptoms ("apathetic hyperthyroidism").
Elderly patients with new-onset atrial fibrillation, worsening angina, or CHF exacerbation should be evaluated for hyperthyroidism.
Maternal Graves' disease, past or present, can lead to neonatal hyperthyroidism due to transplacental transfer of thyroid-stimulating antibodies.
The likelihood of adverse pregnancy outcomes is increased in pregnant patients with hyperthyroidism, including: preeclampsia (OR = 1.78), preterm birth (OR = 1.81) and ICU admission (OR = 3.70).
RAI is contraindicated in pregnant women as it crosses the placenta and may cause hypothyroidism in the fetus; it is also contraindicated in nursing women.
Pregnancy should be avoided for 6 months following RAI ablation.

MMI has rarely been reported to cause aplasia cutis in the fetus and PTU is preferred during pregnancy. PTU has been recommended during lactation due to its lower breast milk concentration; however, severe hepatic dysfunction can occur and may be more frequent with PTU than with MMI.
In a case-control study, there was an association between prenatal exposure to ATDs and several types of birth defects.
A meta analysis confiremed prior studies that PTU is safer in pregnant patients than MMI (OR 0.80, 95%CI 0.69-0.92, P = 0.002, I2 = 41.9%).

Postpartum thyroiditis (PPT) (autoimmune) affects up to 10% of women; these patients may have transient hyperthyroidism followed by hypothyroidism. At present, there are insufficient data to recommend screening of all women for PPT.
Most studies show an association between thyroid antibodies and miscarriage, but causality has not been established.
There is no evidence that treatment of subclinical hyperthyroidism improves pregnancy outcome.
One percent to 5% of newborns of mothers with Graves' disease have hyperthyroidism due to transplacental passage of maternal stimulating TSH receptor antibodies.
Children may present with deteriorating academic performance, acceleration of linear growth, and delayed puberty, in addition to the typical symptoms of hyperthyroidism.

In many centers in the United States, surgery is the preferred therapy for hyperthyroidism in children, but RAI is gaining acceptance as first-line therapy. Long-term studies indicate no increased risk of malignancy or other significant adverse conditions in children (or offspring of patients) treated with RAI for hyperthyroidism.
Relapse rates are high when treated with anti-thyroid drugs, nearly 80% after 2 years. Treatment of Graves' disease with methimazole is therefore recommended for 36 months in children.
In a retrospective review of 34 thyrotoxic children in New Zealand, 32 had Graves' disease and 2 had MNG. More than one-third of children with Graves' disease achieved long-term remission with ATDs.
Children treated successfully for hyperthyroidism have no long-term growth compromise.
